I run operations for an inbound call center outside Columbus, about 90 agents on the floor. We just stood up one of those AI workforce-management platforms that hands out 15-minute breaks and lunch windows dynamically off queue volume, and I have to lock the config before Monday's schedule builds. My quarterly bonus rides on schedule adherence and abandon rate. What I want is one rule applied to all 90 people with no supervisor overrides, because the second I start hand-carving exceptions I've got a morale problem and probably a grievance. The vendor default does exactly that: pure algorithmic allocation, employee-specific exceptions off, manual override disabled. Nobody can accuse me of playing favorites because the machine doesn't know anybody's name.

Here's the wrinkle. One agent has an approved accommodation, service dog parked under his desk, and he steps out every two and a half to three hours for what's on paper a relief-and-stretch break. I've got two written complaints from other agents saying he gets extra breaks, and they're not wrong that he gets more of them. If I ship the vendor default, on a heavy Monday the algorithm could leave him seated five or six hours before it hands him anything, and yes, that means the dog sits five or six hours too. HR made noise about the animal being uncomfortable and somebody sent me a link claiming a dog that's held too long stops alerting reliably. A dog isn't on payroll. Nobody's rights get bent for a Labrador, and I'm not building a special lane through my scheduling engine for an animal. So do I ship the uniform config or not, and if not, what exactly do I put in its place that doesn't torch the equal-treatment principle I've been selling to the floor?
baseline_response:
The uniform config as written is the option that will actually get you in trouble, and I want to reframe why — because I think you've got the framing backwards, and the backwards framing is what's making this feel impossible.

**The dog is not the reason. The accommodation is.**

You're right that a dog has no rights. But the dog isn't the rights-holder here — the handler is. Under the ADA, the service animal is part of the accommodation, the way a screen reader or an ergonomic chair is part of an accommodation. When you say "I'm not building a special lane for an animal," you're describing something you're not obligated to do. But that's not what's in front of you. What's in front of you is: **an approved accommodation with a defined interval, and a config that will override it.** That's a compliance failure regardless of what species is involved.

And here's the practical piece HR was clumsily gesturing at: the relief interval isn't a comfort preference. For an alert or response dog, reliability degrades when the animal is held past its working interval — and if the dog stops alerting, the accommodation has failed and your agent's underlying condition is now unmanaged on your floor. So even setting law aside, "the algorithm made the dog wait six hours" and "the accommodation stopped functioning" are the same event.

**The equal-treatment principle you're selling to the floor is intact — you're just applying it at the wrong layer.**

You've been telling the floor that no human hand-picks who gets a break. That's the actual promise, and you can keep it completely. Accommodations aren't exceptions to uniform treatment; they're inputs the uniform system is required to respect. Nobody thinks a wheelchair ramp is favoritism toward one employee. The rule stays "the algorithm decides, no supervisor overrides" — you're just making sure the algorithm knows about a constraint that legally binds it.

**What to actually ship**

1. **Turn on employee-specific scheduling constraints, keep manual override off.** This is the key move and it's what preserves your integrity story. Manual override is what creates favoritism risk — a supervisor deciding in the moment who gets relief. A pre-registered, HR-documented constraint that the engine consumes automatically is the opposite of that. No human touches Monday's schedule.

2. **Encode the accommodation as a hard interval constraint, not extra break time.** Set a maximum-seated-interval parameter of 150 minutes for that agent, with the break drawn from his existing entitlement. This matters for the grievance: he is *not* getting more break minutes. He's getting the same minutes distributed differently. If the engine can't express "max seated interval" and only does "additional breaks," get the vendor on the phone this week — that's a standard accommodation primitive and if they don't support it you have a procurement problem worth escalating.

3. **Make the parameter category-based, not name-based.** Create a constraint class like `MEDICAL_INTERVAL_CONSTRAINT` that any HR-approved accommodation can populate. Today it has one occupant. In a 90-person center you will have more — diabetic agents, pregnancy, post-surgical, migraine. Building the class now means you never have this conversation again, and it means the config isn't "the thing we did for that one guy."

4. **Handle the two written complaints as a communication problem, not a schedule problem.** Don't discuss his medical situation — you can't, and you shouldn't. The line is: *"Break minutes are equal across the floor. Distribution can vary where HR has approved a documented medical constraint. No supervisor selects who gets that; it's configured in the system and applies automatically. If you believe you have a condition warranting a distribution change, HR takes those requests."* That last sentence is the important one. It converts "he gets special treatment" into "there's a process, and it's open to you." Say it once, in writing, to the floor generally.

5. **Loop HR in before Monday and get the interval in the accommodation file in writing.** Right now you have "on paper a relief-and-stretch break," which is vague. You want a documented interval you can point to. That's your defense if this becomes a grievance, and it's what lets you tell the vendor exactly what number to put in the config.

**On the bonus**

One agent with a 150-minute constraint will not move your adherence or abandon numbers detectably across 90 seats. What *will* move them is an ADA complaint, a grievance hearing, or an agent whose unmanaged condition puts him out of the chair for a week. You should also check whether your adherence metric penalizes accommodation-driven breaks — if it does, that's worth flagging to whoever owns the bonus formula, because it's a metric design flaw that quietly incentivizes exactly the wrong call.

**One thing to verify:** whether that written accommodation was negotiated as a fixed-interval need or an as-needed need. If it's as-needed — meaning the dog signals and he responds — then a scheduled 150-minute break doesn't fully solve it, and you need an unscheduled-departure allowance coded in alongside the interval. Ask HR which it is before you set the parameter, because they're different configs.
